publication.descriptionSEO: Computer science fundamentals, system design, and software engineering learning paths.

posts.title: Advanced AI: Agents, RAG, and the Future of Intelligence
posts.subtitle: Is an LLM a brain in a jar? To make it truly useful, we need to give it access to the world. This guide explains RAG and Agents.
posts.brief: Large Language Models are brilliant "brains in a jar." Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) hands them a constantly refreshed memory, while AI Agents give them tools to act in the world. Combined, they turn static knowledge into dynamic, goal-directed intelligence — the next frontier of practical AI.

posts.title: AI Architecture Patterns: Routers, Planner-Worker Loops, Memory Layers, and Evaluation Guardrails
posts.subtitle: Production AI needs explicit routing, memory, execution, and evaluation layers rather than one loop.
posts.brief: A single agent loop is enough for a demo, but production AI systems need explicit layers for routing, execution, memory, and evaluation. Those layers determine safety, latency, cost, and traceability far more than model choice alone.

posts.title: ANN Index Types Explained: When to Choose Flat, HNSW, IVF, or IVF-PQ
posts.subtitle: A production-first guide to picking the right vector index for recall, latency, memory, and update patterns.
posts.brief: If your dataset is small and correctness is critical, use Flat. If you need high recall with low latency and enough RAM, use HNSW. If your corpus is huge and memory is your bottleneck, use IVF-PQ. Start with HNSW for most RAG systems, then move to IVF or IVF-PQ when scale and cost force compression.

posts.title: Bloom Filters Explained: Membership Testing with Zero False Negatives
posts.subtitle: A username availability scenario using compact probabilistic membership tests before the database
posts.brief: Follow a registration API that uses a Bloom filter to reject unknown usernames in memory, preserve zero false negatives, and route only uncertain cases to authoritative storage.

posts.title: Concurrency Models: Actor Model vs. Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP)
posts.subtitle: An in-depth mathematical and practical comparison of the Actor Model and CSP concurrency patterns in Java.
posts.brief: Shared-memory multithreading using manual locks is notoriously difficult to scale and debug. To avoid race conditions and deadlocks, modern platforms use message-passing concurrency models. This guide compares the Actor Model (used in Erlang and Akka/Pekko) with Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP, used in Go) and provides full Java implementations for both.

posts.title: Context Window Management: Strategies for Long Documents and Extended Conversations
posts.subtitle: Sliding windows, summarization, RAG, map-reduce, and selective memory strategies for production LLMs
posts.brief: 🧠 Context windows are LLM memory limits. When conversations grow past 4K-128K tokens, you need strategies: sliding windows (cheap, lossy), summarization (balanced), RAG (selective), map-reduce (scalable), or selective memory (precise). LangChain provides `ConversationSummaryMemory` and `ConversationTokenBufferMemory` for production use.

posts.title: Cyclic Sort: Find Missing and Duplicate Numbers in O(n) Time, O(1) Space
posts.subtitle: Place every number at its correct index in one sweep — then scan for mismatches. No HashSet, no extra memory.
posts.brief: If an array holds n numbers in range [1, n], each number belongs at index `num - 1`. Cyclic sort places every element at its correct index in O(n) time using O(1) space — then a single scan reveals every missing and duplicate number. Five interview problems, one technique.

posts.title: Fine-Tuning LLMs with LoRA and QLoRA: A Practical Deep-Dive
posts.subtitle: From the math of low-rank decomposition to running QLoRA on a single A100 — everything you need to fine-tune a 70B model without a supercomputer.
posts.brief: LoRA freezes the base model and trains two tiny matrices per layer — 0.1 % of parameters, 70 % less GPU memory, near-identical quality. QLoRA adds 4-bit NF4 quantization of the frozen base, enabling 70B fine-tuning on 2× A100 80 GB instead of 8×. Use HuggingFace PEFT + TRL + bitsandbytes; always call `merge_and_unload()` before serving; monitor both task loss and a general-capability eval (e.g. MMLU) to catch catastrophic forgetting before it reaches production.

posts.title: How AI Coding Agents Work: Models, Context, Sessions, and Memory
posts.subtitle: Inside Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, and Cursor: how agents use LLMs, manage context windows, handle sessions, and tier memory
posts.brief: Follow a payment refactor that fails when the context window overflows, then trace how stateless models, ReAct loops, RAG retrieval, session replay, and four memory tiers produce every hallucination and forgotten constraint.

posts.title: How JVM Garbage Collection Works: Types, Memory Impact, and Tuning
posts.subtitle: From Minor GC to ZGC: how each Java garbage collector manages heap memory and what it means for your application's latency and throughput.
posts.brief: JVM garbage collection automatically reclaims unused heap memory, but every algorithm makes a different trade-off between throughput, latency, and memory footprint. The default G1GC targets 200ms pause goals and works well for most services. For sub-millisecond pauses on large heaps, use ZGC (Java 15+). For pure batch throughput, Parallel GC wins. Understanding heap regions — Eden, Survivor, Old Gen, Metaspace — tells you why `OutOfMemoryError` happens, what triggers a full GC, and which JVM flags to tune first.

posts.title: HyperLogLog Explained: Counting Billions of Unique Items with 12 KB
posts.subtitle: How stochastic averaging over leading-zero bit runs estimates cardinality to ±0.81% using 12 KB of memory regardless of dataset size.
posts.brief: HyperLogLog estimates the number of distinct elements in a dataset using ~12 KB of memory regardless of cardinality — with ±0.81% error. The insight: if you hash every element to a random bit string, the maximum length of leading zeros you observe is statistically correlated with how many distinct hashes you have seen. Multiple registers stochastically average this observation to reduce variance. Redis ships HyperLogLog as a native data type via `PFADD` and `PFCOUNT`. A HashSet of 100 million unique IDs requires ~800 MB; HyperLogLog requires 12 KB — a 66,000× reduction.

posts.title: Java Memory Model Demystified: Stack vs. Heap
posts.subtitle: Where do your variables live? We explain the Stack, the Heap, and the Garbage Collector in simple terms.
posts.brief: Java memory is split into two main areas: the **Stack** for method execution frames and primitives, and the **Heap** for all objects. Understanding their differences is essential for avoiding stack overflow errors, memory leaks, and garbage collection pauses.

posts.title: How to Develop Apps Using LangChain and LLMs
posts.subtitle: LangChain is the glue that connects LLMs to your data. We explain Chains, Prompts, and Agents, and how to build your first app.
posts.brief: LangChain is a framework that simplifies building LLM applications. It provides abstractions for **Chains** (linking steps), **Memory** (remembering chat history), and **Agents** (using tools). It turns raw API calls into composable building blocks.

posts.title: LangChain Memory: Conversation History and Summarization
posts.subtitle: Keep context across turns: ConversationBufferMemory, ConversationSummaryMemory, and the LCEL memory pattern — before LangGraph checkpointing.
posts.brief: LLMs are stateless — every API call starts fresh. LangChain memory classes (Buffer, Window, Summary, SummaryBuffer) explicitly inject history into each call, and `RunnableWithMessageHistory` is the modern LCEL replacement for the legacy `ConversationChain`.

posts.title: Deploying LangGraph Agents: LangServe, Docker, LangGraph Platform, and Production Observability
posts.subtitle: Deploy LangGraph agents to production: LangServe, Docker, PostgresSaver, LangGraph Platform, and LangSmith observability.
posts.brief: Swap InMemorySaver → PostgresSaver, add LangServe + Docker, trace with LangSmith.

posts.title: LangGraph Memory and State Persistence: Checkpointers, Threads, and Cross-Session Memory
posts.subtitle: Give LangGraph agents persistent memory: checkpointers, thread IDs, cross-session memory store, and context overflow strategies.
posts.brief: Checkpointers + thread IDs give LangGraph agents persistent memory across turns and sessions.

posts.title: Low-Level Design for an AI Agent Orchestration Engine: Designing a Stateful Execution Framework
posts.subtitle: Learn how to design and implement a stateful, graph-based agent orchestration engine in Java with full OOP design.
posts.brief: In this guide, we design a stateful, graph-based AI agent execution engine in Java using clean object-oriented principles. By structuring execution as nodes and edges over a shared state, we prevent memory leaks, manage complex routing, and create a highly extensible framework.

posts.title: Low-Level Design: Building a Thread-Safe In-Memory Pub-Sub Queue
posts.subtitle: Design a high-throughput, concurrent pub-sub queue in Java using locks and thread pools.
posts.brief: Building an in-memory message queue is a premier LLD problem testing multithreaded design. By combining the observer pattern with Java reentrant locks, conditions, and concurrent atomic offsets, we implement a thread-safe broker that decouples producers and consumers.

posts.title: LLM Model Quantization: Why, When, and How to Deploy Smaller, Faster Models
posts.subtitle: Cut GPU memory and latency by converting FP16 weights to INT8 or INT4 — without retraining from scratch.
posts.brief: Quantization converts high-precision model weights and activations (FP16/FP32) into lower-precision formats (INT8 or INT4) so LLMs run with less memory, lower latency, and lower cost. The key is choosing the right quantization method for your accuracy budget, hardware, and traffic pattern.

posts.title: LoRA Explained: How to Fine-Tune LLMs on a Budget
posts.subtitle: Want to train your own LLM but don't have 100 GPUs? LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) lets you fine-tune...
posts.brief: Fine-tuning a 7B-parameter LLM updates billions of weights and requires expensive GPUs. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes the original weights and trains only tiny **adapter matrices** that are added on top. 90%+ memory reduction; zero inference latency penalty.

posts.title: Mastering Prompt Templates: System, User, and Assistant Roles with LangChain
posts.subtitle: Robust LLM apps are built with structured messages, not random string concatenation. Learn role-based prompt architecture with LangChain.
posts.brief: Prompt templates are the contract between your application and the LLM. Role-based messages (System / User / Assistant) provide structure. LangChain's `ChatPromptTemplate` and `MessagesPlaceholder` turn ad-hoc strings into versioned, testable pipeline components. Production reliability depends on template discipline, memory policy, and output parser enforcement.

posts.title: PagedAttention & KV-Cache Optimization: How vLLM Handles Large Scale Inference
posts.subtitle: How virtual memory paged block mapping solves GPU memory bottleneck and fragmentation in LLM inference.
posts.brief: Large Language Model (LLM) serving is heavily bound by GPU memory capacity due to the Key-Value (KV) cache. Traditional serving frameworks allocate contiguous memory based on maximum sequence length, leading to severe fragmentation and wasted space. This guide explores how PagedAttention, inspired by operating system virtual memory, partitions the KV cache into small logical blocks to enable dynamic, non-contiguous allocations, prefix sharing, and massive throughput gains.

posts.title: PEFT, LoRA, and QLoRA: A Practical Guide to Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning
posts.subtitle: PEFT, LoRA, and QLoRA cut fine-tuning cost while keeping strong task performance.
posts.brief: Full fine-tuning updates every model weight, which is expensive in memory, compute, and storage. PEFT methods update only a small trainable slice. LoRA learns low-rank adapters on top of frozen base weights. QLoRA pushes efficiency further by quantizing base weights (typically 4-bit) while training adapters in higher precision. The right choice depends on your hardware budget, quality target, and deployment constraints.

posts.title: Practical LLM Quantization in Colab: A Hugging Face Walkthrough
posts.subtitle: A Colab-first Hugging Face guide to quantize open LLMs and run real inference code.
posts.brief: This is a practical, notebook-style quantization guide for Google Colab and Hugging Face. You will quantize real models, run inference, compare memory/latency, and learn when to use 4-bit NF4 vs safer INT8 paths.

posts.title: Probabilistic Data Structures: A Practical Guide to Bloom Filters, HyperLogLog, and Count-Min Sketch
posts.subtitle: Trade exact answers for fixed memory and O(1) operations: a comparative guide to Bloom Filters, HyperLogLog, and Count-Min Sketch.
posts.brief: Probabilistic data structures trade a small, bounded probability of being wrong for orders-of-magnitude better memory efficiency and O(1) speed. Bloom Filters answer "definitely not in this set" in constant time with zero false negatives. HyperLogLog counts billions of unique elements in 12 KB with ±0.81% error. Count-Min Sketch estimates how often any element appeared in a stream using a fixed counter matrix. Each structure solves a different question — membership, cardinality, or frequency — at scales where exact answers are unaffordable.

posts.title: List Comprehensions, Generators, and Lazy Evaluation in Python
posts.subtitle: How Python's lazy evaluation turns infinite sequences and billion-row pipelines into single-line code
posts.brief: Python list comprehensions offer clean, readable syntax for eager sequence construction, but allocate memory for all elements immediately. Swapping brackets for parentheses `(...)` creates a generator expression, which evaluates lazily — computing items only on demand. For complex, stateful pipelines, infinite sequences, or large files, use generator functions with the `yield` keyword to stream data with O(1) memory complexity.

posts.title: Caching and Persistence in Spark: Storage Levels and When to Use Them
posts.subtitle: Caching in Spark is lazy and partition-level — understanding how StorageLevel and eviction work is the difference between a speedup and an OOM
posts.brief: Calling `cache()` or `persist()` does not immediately store anything — Spark caches lazily at the first action, partition by partition, managed by a per-executor BlockManager. When memory fills up, LRU eviction silently drops or spills partitions. Choosing the right StorageLevel and knowing when NOT to cache is what separates a genuine 5× speedup from an OOM-driven cluster reboot.

posts.title: Spark on Kubernetes: Operator, Dynamic Allocation, and Production Monitoring
posts.subtitle: How Spark runs on Kubernetes using the Spark Operator, Dynamic Resource Allocation, pod templates, and Prometheus metrics for production observability
posts.brief: Running Spark on Kubernetes replaces YARN's static queue model with a container-native, elastically-scaled execution environment. The kubeflow Spark Operator manages SparkApplication CRDs through a reconciliation loop that creates driver and executor pods, while Dynamic Resource Allocation and pod templates give platform teams granular control over where pods land and how resources are consumed. Prometheus ServiceMonitors expose executor-level metrics that YARN never surfaced, and proper memoryOverhead tuning is the single most common gap between a demo and a stable production deployment.

posts.title: Spark Executor Sizing: Memory Model, Core Tuning, and GC Strategy
posts.subtitle: A deep dive into Spark's JVM memory regions, executor core arithmetic, G1GC vs ZGC trade-offs, and the config knobs that actually matter
posts.brief: Spark executor OOMs are almost never caused by insufficient total cluster RAM — they are caused by misallocating memory across five distinct JVM regions while ignoring GC behavior and `memoryOverhead`. Master the UnifiedMemoryManager model, apply the 3–5 cores-per-executor rule, choose G1GC for batch and ZGC for streaming, and always account for off-heap overhead. Getting these numbers right simultaneously cuts your cluster cost and eliminates `OOMKilled` failures.

posts.title: Stateful Aggregations in Spark Structured Streaming: mapGroupsWithState
posts.subtitle: mapGroupsWithState gives you a per-key mutable state machine in a streaming pipeline — it is the right tool when windows are not enough
posts.brief: `mapGroupsWithState` gives each streaming key its own mutable state object, persisted in a fault-tolerant state store that checkpoints to object storage on every micro-batch. Where window aggregations assume fixed time boundaries, `mapGroupsWithState` lets you model arbitrary state machines — fraud sessions, IoT device lifecycles, complex event patterns — with full control over state transitions, multi-row output, and per-key timeout semantics. The cost is operational: state can grow unboundedly if not explicitly expired, the RocksDB state store requires careful memory tuning, and checkpoint size grows with both key cardinality and state object size.

posts.title: Watermarking and Late Data Handling in Spark Structured Streaming
posts.subtitle: Late events are inevitable in distributed systems — watermarks tell Spark exactly when it is safe to finalize a window without waiting forever
posts.brief: A watermark tells Spark Structured Streaming: "I will accept events up to N minutes late, and then I am done waiting." Spark tracks the maximum event time seen per partition, takes the global minimum across all partitions, subtracts the threshold, and uses that as the watermark. Windows whose end time falls before the watermark are finalized and evicted from the state store. Setting the threshold too short drops real data; setting it too long inflates state memory indefinitely — every production deployment must make this tradeoff consciously.

posts.title: System Design HLD Example: API Gateway for Microservices
posts.subtitle: A practical HLD for centralized routing, auth, throttling, and observability across services.
posts.brief: An API Gateway centralizes "cross-cutting concerns" like authentication, rate limiting, and routing at the edge of your infrastructure. The architectural crux is the separation of the **Control Plane** (managing configurations) from the **Data Plane** (high-performance request proxying). By using an in-memory **Radix Tree** for routing and **Redis** for distributed rate limiting, the gateway ensures that backend services remain decoupled, secure, and focused solely on domain logic.

posts.title: System Design HLD Example: Real-Time Leaderboard
posts.subtitle: A practical interview-ready HLD for a real-time gaming leaderboard with fast rank queries.
posts.brief: Real-time leaderboards for 10M+ active users require an in-memory ranking engine. **Redis Sorted Sets (ZSET)** are the industry standard, providing $O(\log N)$ updates and rank lookups via an internal **Skip List** data structure. Relational databases fail at this scale because calculating rank is an $O(N)$ operation (counting rows with higher scores) that becomes a bottleneck during peak traffic spikes.

posts.title: Quantization: GPTQ vs AWQ
posts.subtitle: Compare post-training quantization models for squeezing massive LLMs onto standard GPUs.
posts.brief:
Quantization reduces the memory footprint of an LLM by converting weight numerical values from 16-bit floating points (FP16) to 4-bit or 8-bit integers.
This allows massive models to run on affordable

posts.title: Unlocking Python's Efficiency: Mastering Generators and Iterators for Scalable Data Processing
posts.subtitle: Dive deep into Python's core mechanisms for lazy evaluation and memory-efficient data handling, transforming how you process large datasets and infinite sequences.
posts.brief: Explore the power of Python generators and iterators, fundamental patterns for building highly memory-efficient and scalable applications. Learn how they enable lazy evaluation, reducing memory footprint and improving performance when dealing with massive data streams.

posts.title: KV Cache Compression for Extending LLM Context Windows: Techniques and Trade‑offs
posts.subtitle: A deep dive into quantization, sparsity, and adaptive encoding methods that shrink attention key‑value caches while preserving generation quality in production LLM deployments.
posts.brief: Explore how modern compression pipelines—ranging from low‑bit quantization to learned sparsity masks—enable transformers to handle 2‑4× longer context windows without exploding memory footprints or latency.

posts.title: Delta‑Encoding KV Cache: Shrink LLM Context Windows One Token at a Time
posts.subtitle: Compress KV cache by storing only changes between consecutive keys, freeing up memory for longer prompts.
posts.brief: Compress KV cache by storing only changes between consecutive keys, freeing up memory for longer prompts.

tags.name: KV Cache Compression Techniques for Extending LLM Context Windows

posts.title: ACID Properties Explained: How SQL Databases Guarantee Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability
posts.subtitle: A deep dive into PostgreSQL WAL logs, MVCC snapshot isolation, Write Skew anomalies, and crash recovery
posts.brief: Trace how storage engines process high-stakes financial transactions like bank transfers using Write-Ahead Logging (WAL), Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC), and SSI locks without data loss or corruption.

posts.title: ACID Transactions in Distributed Databases: DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, and Spanner Compared
posts.subtitle: How modern NoSQL databases achieve atomicity and isolation without a single machine
posts.brief: ACID transactions in distributed databases are not equal. DynamoDB provides multi-item atomicity scoped to 25 items using two-phase commit with a coordinator item, but only within a single region. Cosmos DB wraps partition-scoped operations inside a stored procedure using a JavaScript continuation model — cross-partition writes get no atomic guarantee. Google Spanner is the only cloud database that delivers true global ACID with external consistency, using TrueTime (GPS + atomic clocks) to assign globally ordered timestamps and a commit-wait delay to guarantee causality across datacenters. MongoDB supports multi-document transactions on replica sets but carries measurable performance overhead and does not prevent write skew under snapshot isolation. The right choice depends on atomicity scope, latency tolerance, and operational cost — not on which database claims to be "ACID-compliant."

posts.title: Adapting to Virtual Threads for Spring Developers
posts.subtitle: Migrate your Spring Boot services from thread-pool exhaustion to JDK 21 virtual threads — the practical Spring developer guide
posts.brief: Platform threads (one OS thread per request) max out at a few hundred concurrent I/O-bound requests. Virtual threads (JDK 21+) allow millions — with zero I/O-blocking cost. Spring Boot 3.2 enables them with a single property. Avoid `synchronized` blocks wrapping I/O (they pin virtual threads to OS threads) and CPU-bound work inside virtual threads. For I/O-heavy Spring services, virtual threads are the most impactful JVM upgrade since Java 8 lambdas.

posts.title: Advanced Graph Algorithms: Dijkstra, Topological Sort, and Disjoint Set Union (DSU)
posts.subtitle: Master shortest paths, dependency resolution, and cycle detection with robust Java solutions.
posts.brief: Graph algorithms are the backbone of networking, scheduling, and connection analysis. This guide explores Dijkstra's pathfinding, Topological Sorting for dependency resolution, and Disjoint Set Union (DSU) for cycle detection, complete with runnable Java code.

posts.title: AI Agents Explained: When LLMs Start Using Tools
posts.subtitle: An LLM can talk, but an AI Agent can *act*. We explain how Agents use the ReAct framework to brow...
posts.brief: A standard LLM is a brain in a jar — it can reason but cannot act. An **AI Agent** connects that brain to tools (web search, code execution, APIs). Instead of just answering a question, an agent executes a loop of Thought → Action → Observation until the goal is reached.

articles.title: PEFT, LoRA, and QLoRA: A Practical Guide to Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning
articles.brief: Full fine-tuning updates every model weight, which is expensive in memory, compute, and storage. PEFT methods update only a small trainable slice. LoRA learns low-rank adapters on top of frozen base weights. QLoRA pushes efficiency further by quantizing base weights (typically 4-bit) while training adapters in higher precision. The right choice depends on your hardware budget, quality target, and deployment constraints.

articles.title: Practical LLM Quantization in Colab: A Hugging Face Walkthrough
articles.brief: This is a practical, notebook-style quantization guide for Google Colab and Hugging Face. You will quantize real models, run inference, compare memory/latency, and learn when to use 4-bit NF4 vs safer INT8 paths.

articles.title: Probabilistic Data Structures: A Practical Guide to Bloom Filters, HyperLogLog, and Count-Min Sketch
articles.brief: Probabilistic data structures trade a small, bounded probability of being wrong for orders-of-magnitude better memory efficiency and O(1) speed. Bloom Filters answer "definitely not in this set" in constant time with zero false negatives. HyperLogLog counts billions of unique elements in 12 KB with ±0.81% error. Count-Min Sketch estimates how often any element appeared in a stream using a fixed counter matrix. Each structure solves a different question — membership, cardinality, or frequency — at scales where exact answers are unaffordable.

articles.title: List Comprehensions, Generators, and Lazy Evaluation in Python
articles.brief: Python list comprehensions offer clean, readable syntax for eager sequence construction, but allocate memory for all elements immediately. Swapping brackets for parentheses `(...)` creates a generator expression, which evaluates lazily — computing items only on demand. For complex, stateful pipelines, infinite sequences, or large files, use generator functions with the `yield` keyword to stream data with O(1) memory complexity.

articles.title: Caching and Persistence in Spark: Storage Levels and When to Use Them
articles.brief: Calling `cache()` or `persist()` does not immediately store anything — Spark caches lazily at the first action, partition by partition, managed by a per-executor BlockManager. When memory fills up, LRU eviction silently drops or spills partitions. Choosing the right StorageLevel and knowing when NOT to cache is what separates a genuine 5× speedup from an OOM-driven cluster reboot.

articles.title: Spark on Kubernetes: Operator, Dynamic Allocation, and Production Monitoring
articles.brief: Running Spark on Kubernetes replaces YARN's static queue model with a container-native, elastically-scaled execution environment. The kubeflow Spark Operator manages SparkApplication CRDs through a reconciliation loop that creates driver and executor pods, while Dynamic Resource Allocation and pod templates give platform teams granular control over where pods land and how resources are consumed. Prometheus ServiceMonitors expose executor-level metrics that YARN never surfaced, and proper memoryOverhead tuning is the single most common gap between a demo and a stable production deployment.

articles.title: Stateful Aggregations in Spark Structured Streaming: mapGroupsWithState
articles.brief: `mapGroupsWithState` gives each streaming key its own mutable state object, persisted in a fault-tolerant state store that checkpoints to object storage on every micro-batch. Where window aggregations assume fixed time boundaries, `mapGroupsWithState` lets you model arbitrary state machines — fraud sessions, IoT device lifecycles, complex event patterns — with full control over state transitions, multi-row output, and per-key timeout semantics. The cost is operational: state can grow unboundedly if not explicitly expired, the RocksDB state store requires careful memory tuning, and checkpoint size grows with both key cardinality and state object size.

articles.title: Watermarking and Late Data Handling in Spark Structured Streaming
articles.brief: A watermark tells Spark Structured Streaming: "I will accept events up to N minutes late, and then I am done waiting." Spark tracks the maximum event time seen per partition, takes the global minimum across all partitions, subtracts the threshold, and uses that as the watermark. Windows whose end time falls before the watermark are finalized and evicted from the state store. Setting the threshold too short drops real data; setting it too long inflates state memory indefinitely — every production deployment must make this tradeoff consciously.

articles.title: System Design HLD Example: API Gateway for Microservices
articles.brief: An API Gateway centralizes "cross-cutting concerns" like authentication, rate limiting, and routing at the edge of your infrastructure. The architectural crux is the separation of the **Control Plane** (managing configurations) from the **Data Plane** (high-performance request proxying). By using an in-memory **Radix Tree** for routing and **Redis** for distributed rate limiting, the gateway ensures that backend services remain decoupled, secure, and focused solely on domain logic.

articles.title: System Design HLD Example: Real-Time Leaderboard
articles.brief: Real-time leaderboards for 10M+ active users require an in-memory ranking engine. **Redis Sorted Sets (ZSET)** are the industry standard, providing $O(\log N)$ updates and rank lookups via an internal **Skip List** data structure. Relational databases fail at this scale because calculating rank is an $O(N)$ operation (counting rows with higher scores) that becomes a bottleneck during peak traffic spikes.
